newsitem.title: SPAIN: France reassures Spain of support for EMU bid.
newsitem.headline: France reassures Spain of support for EMU bid.

text.p: France reaffirmed on Monday its support for Spain's bid to join founders of a European single currency, casting aside doubts about its neighbour's fitness to be counted among the continent's economic heavyweights.

French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis emerged from a meeting with Spanish Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato saying he was impressed by Spain's efforts to prepare for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"France is confident of the determination of the Spanish government to meet the convergence criteria in 1997 and to be in the group of nations launching EMU in 1999," Arthuis said.
Arthuis brushed aside reservations raised recently by a top German official and bankers about Spain's long-term economic health.
"I am impressed by the efficiency of Minister Rato's (convergence) policy," he said at a joint news conference in Madrid.

In February, German Finance Secretary Juergen Stark said some countries did not have the economic track record to join in the euro launch. Although he named no names, market participants took it as a reference to Italy, Spain and Portugal.

But Spain has pressed its economic clean-up project and now fulfils long-term interest rate, inflation and currency stability criteria for EMU. It is also considered to be on schedule for deficit and debt requirements.
Both ministers confirmed their commitment to meeting EMU convergence criteria and to the single currency calendar.
"We emphasised again the strong willingness of both sides to form part of the first wave of countries to join EMU in 1999," Rato said.
Arthuis added he was confident there would be no delay in the launch. "The deadlines for the euro will be met," he said.

Spain, eager to dismiss suggestions that its participation would weaken a single currency, said the decision on who participates in the EMU launch on January 1, 1999 would be based solely on the Maastricht Treaty convergence criteria.
"Access to EMU will be given country by country and (on the basis of) the fulfilment of the treaty criteria".
Germany is believed to be very reluctant to allow Italy, Spain and Portugal into EMU when it is first launched, fearing this would undermine the credibility of the new currency.

But economists have said they doubt Germany, meant to be Europe's model economy, can slash its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year as required by the convergence criteria.

Any overshooting by Bonn would make it harder to exclude other countries. Europe's leaders are due to decide in early 1998, on the basis of fiscal and monetary performances in 1997, which countries can join the single currency.
The ministers said they had also discussed proposals for an informal stability council to co-ordinate economic policies after the launch of a monetary union.

"Spain is studying the French proposal in the belief that it will be informal and we agreed that it should be an instrument that strengthens European credibility and does not divide countries," Rato said.
However, he added Spain had not yet made a decision on the proposal.

The idea came under attack earlier this year, notably from some members of the German Bundesbank, who feared such a council might be used to undermine the independence of the future European Central Bank.
France, which first proposed the council as a counterweight to the European Central Bank, now appears to have worn down resistance on the grounds it will have very little power.
